owner.tagline: I design parts in CAD, print and machine them, and test whether they actually work in someone's hands.
about: I'm a sophomore studying Mechanical Engineering at the University of Michigan. Most of my hands-on work so far has come out of ENGR 100: Socially Engaged Engineering - Design of Adaptive Gaming Technology, where the whole point was to build gaming hardware that people with different physical abilities can actually use.

My first project was an individual build: I took a provided CAD file for a game controller, measured a physical controller and my own hand, and modified the design in Onshape until it fit me. The biggest change I made was adding hand grips so the controller stays comfortable over a long session. I printed the case and buttons, then soldered and wired the interior and programmed the Arduino board that drives it.

My second project was a team build. Three of us designed an adaptive controller for a user with hemiparesis, who has significant weakness in her left hand and wanted to play Mario Kart with her family. We put the joystick and the drift and item buttons under the right hand, gave the left hand one large low-force acceleration button she can just rest on, and built a flat wooden case so the controller sits on a table instead of being held. We interviewed two professionals in the field, presented the prototype to them, and revised the design from their feedback before the final version.

Outside of coursework I'm on the Chassis sub-team for Michigan Chem-E-Car, where I do CAD and fabrication work at the Wilson Center on the mechanical parts of the car. I also work part-time as a Math Proctor for the Mathematics Department.

What I like most is the part where the model meets the material: a keycap that has to be dimensioned exactly right to snap onto a switch, or a case that teaches you the hard way that precision woodcutting is not a skill you pick up in an afternoon.

items: Modifying an existing CAD file to a new requirement
Designing to hand measurements and reach specifications
Tolerancing parts to fit off-the-shelf switches and sticks
FDM 3D printing: cases, keycaps, stick caps, supports
Woodworking: cutting, drilling, screwing, gluing a case
Shop machine use at the Wilson Student Team Project Center
Wiring and harness routing inside an enclosure
Arduino / Pro Micro programming for controller input
Troubleshooting dead buttons and weak solder joints
Translating user needs into measurable specifications
Verification testing with calipers, rulers, and a force gauge
Usability testing and incorporating participant feedback
Interviewing subject-matter professionals and revising a design
Technical report writing and team collaboration

projects.summary: A three-person team build of a game controller for a user with hemiparesis who has significant weakness in her left hand. The joystick and the drift and item buttons sit under the right hand; the left hand gets one large, low-force acceleration button to rest on. metrics: Acceleration button actuation force measured at 0.96 N against a 2 N maximum
Drift and item buttons verified within 2 cm of each other
Joystick verified within 9.5 cm of the button cluster
Usability tested with 5 participants for about 20 minutes each
Six custom 3D-printed parts: stick cap, two keycaps, acceleration button, and three supports
